---
title: "Trace and Determinant"
---

\newcommand{\trace}{\mathrm{trace}}



### Trace

If $A$ is an $n\times n$ square matrix with entries in a field $F$, then
the *trace* $\trace(A)$ is the sum $\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{ii}$ of the diagonal elements of $A$.


**Proposition:** If $A$ and $B$ are $n\times n$ matrices over $F$,
then $\trace(AB)=\trace(BA)$.

**Proof:** Let $C=AB$ and $D=BA$.  Then 
$$
c_{ij} = \sum_{k} a_{ik}b_{kj}.
$$

and 

$$
d_{ij} = \sum_{k} b_{ik}a_{kj}
$$

Now
$$
\trace(AB) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} c_{ii} = \sum_{i}\sum_{k} a_{ik}b_{ki}
=\sum_{k}\sum_{i} b_{ki}a_{ik} =\sum_{k} d_{kk} = \trace(BA)
$$


Now let $f:V\to V$ be any linear map, where $V$ is a finite dimensional vector space.  Choose a basis $E$ for $V$ and define the trace $\trace(f)$
to be the trace of the matrix $[f]_{E}^{E}$.  

This is a well-defined invariant of $f$ because if we choose a different basis, say $F$, then $[f]_{F}^{F} =[1]_{F}^{E} [f]_{E}^{E}[1]_{E}^{F}$
Thus 
$$
\begin{aligned}
\trace([f]_{F}^{F})&=\trace([1]_{F}^{E}[f]_{E}^{E}[1]_{E}^{F})\\
&=\trace([f]_{E}^{E}[1]_{E}^{F}[1]_{F}^{E})\\
&=\trace([f]_{E}^{E})
\end{aligned}
$$

since $[1]_{F}^{E}[1]_{E}^{F}=[1]_{E}^{E}$ is the identity matrix.
